messages.content: Explain how a language model produces text. Keep the answer under 100 words.

results.output: A language model generates text by predicting the most likely next word based on the input context. It uses patterns learned from vast amounts of training data to assign probabilities to possible word sequences. Starting with an initial prompt, the model selects words iteratively, updating the context with each choice. Advanced models like GPT use neural networks, specifically transformers, to process and understand relationships between words, enabling coherent and contextually relevant text generation. This process continues until a stopping condition, such as a specified length or end token, is met.

Input words are converted to embeddings, processed (commonly by transformer layers with attention) to produce a probability distribution over possible next tokens. Text is generated by repeatedly sampling or selecting the highest-probability token and feeding it back until a stopping condition is reached. Training adjusts weights to match real-world token patterns.

title: Sound is samples: speech out, speech in
concept: Sound is a long list of numbers: amplitude samples taken many thousand times per second. A text-to-speech model generates them, a speech-recognition model turns them back into words, and the round trip lets us measure how much survives.
question: What happened to the transcript as the noise grew louder, and what does that say about trusting speech recognition on a noisy recording?
caveat: The speech is synthetic, one sentence, one run per condition. White noise is a simplified model of real noise; real recordings add accents, music, echo, and overlapping talkers. Pitch and speaking-rate numbers are rough signal measurements.

title: Music is tokens
concept: A melody can be written as a sequence of note-event tokens. A model that predicts the next token can then compose, just as Lab 00 predicted words. Here three kinds of composer are measured with the same music-theory yardstick, and every melody is rendered to real audio that we check by pitch tracking.
question: What did learning from nine tunes change compared with random notes, and what did raising the temperature change?
caveat: Azure offers no music-generation model in this subscription, so this lab uses symbolic notes, a tiny statistical model, and GPT-4o prompted to write notes; it is not how audio models like MusicGen or Lyria work. The corpus is nine simplified public-domain phrases, the synthesizer is a basic harmonic tone generator, and these measurements do not judge whether a melody is beautiful.
exercise: Replace one of the nine phrases in corpus (lib/genai/music-lab.mjs) with another public-domain phrase of exactly 32 eighth-note slots, redeploy, and see which statistics move.

title: Video is frames over time
concept: A video model sees a video as a short list of still frames. How many frames you sample decides what it can know about motion and how many tokens you pay. Sample too sparsely and the video can be genuinely ambiguous, no matter how smart the model is.
question: Which questions about motion can be answered from a handful of frames, and which are impossible no matter how good the model is?
caveat: The video is drawn by our own code, so the right answers are exact, but there are only five tiny clips and one run per model. Azure's only video-generation model (Sora 2) passed its retirement date on 2026-11-02, so this lab studies video understanding from frames, not video generation.

title: Can a model grade a model?
concept: Teams often use one model to grade another model's answers because human review is slow. A judge is itself a model with biases. Because we know the right answers, we can measure whether the judge is accurate, whether it favors the first response it reads, and whether it is fooled by a confident, longer answer.
question: If the same two answers are shown in the opposite order, does the judge change its mind, and what does that mean for using a model as a grader?
caveat: Six simple arithmetic pairs and four equal-quality pairs, one run per judge: enough to illustrate the checks, not to rank the models. Judges can also be wrong in ways that fit their own errors. Always keep a human-checked sample, and swap positions to expose bias.
exercise: Add a pair to truthPairs in lib/genai/judge-lab.mjs where the correct answer is longer and the wrong one is confident. Predict whether each judge notices before you redeploy.
